modalities.name: Chin on the Grass
modalities.tagline: Lie face down on a lawn, eyes open, and add nothing.
modalities.whatItIs: Chin on the Grass is a new, untested idea that pushes Do Nothing meditation away from loving-kindness by bringing the world down to a few inches in front of your eyes. You lie on your front on a blanket outdoors, chin on your hands, eyes open at grass level, and do nothing at all: no wishes, no phrases, no studying what is there and no looking for anything in particular.
modalities.coreIdea: Loving-kindness reaches out toward all beings everywhere, a boundless reach built in the imagination. Here the whole scene is the small patch of ground right in front of your face, seen rather than imagined, and you add nothing to it, not even curiosity.
modalities.whatYouDo: On a dry, mild day you spread a blanket on a lawn or meadow you know is safe, lie on your front with your chin resting on your folded hands, and stay for 15 to 30 minutes with your eyes open at grass level. Your eyes wander or rest as they like, the smell of the earth, the sun or breeze and passing thoughts come and go, and if you catch yourself examining something, naming it or trying to feel something special, you let that go too.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find kindness meditations wordy or effortful and want a plain rest with no task, and anyone who rarely gets down on the ground once childhood is over.
modalities.cautions: Check the spot for ticks, nettles, ants and dog mess, use a blanket and sun protection, and skip it if you have grass allergies or hay fever, if lying face down strains your neck or back, or if there is nowhere you feel safe lying down outdoors. Doing nothing can let low moods or old memories surface, so people with severe depression, trauma or dissociation should talk to a clinician before practicing alone.
modalities.tweet: Lie on your front on a lawn, chin on your hands, eyes open at grass level, for 20 minutes. Nothing to study, name or feel, with the world shrunk to a few inches. Nothing is wanted from you in Chin on the Grass, and it's untested. Check for ticks first.

modalities.name: No Levels, No Records
modalities.tagline: Every sit counts the same, and nothing is kept.
modalities.whatItIs: No Levels, No Records is a new, untested idea that pushes Do Nothing meditation away from concentration practices that build skill toward special states. There is no teacher, no object, no stage to reach and no log. If a lovely or unusual state turns up, you do not try to hold it or get it back next time.
modalities.coreIdea: Jhana is a long-term skill with stages, mastery and a teacher. Here none of that exists, so meditation can never become a ladder to climb or a performance to measure, and each sit counts the same, however it went.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sit alone for 10 to 20 minutes and let whatever happens happen, without choosing anything to focus on or trying to go deeper. Afterward you write nothing down and rate nothing, and if you catch yourself trying to repeat a good sit or avoid a bad one, you let that wish go too.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who have turned meditation into another goal to achieve, or who feel they are always doing it wrong.
modalities.cautions: With no anchor and no teacher some people drift, doze or slide into worry, so keep sits short and stop if they leave you more upset than before. Strong fear, unusual perceptions or a changed sense of self during or after sitting are reasons to stop and talk to a clinician, and people with psychosis, bipolar disorder, dissociation or severe trauma should get advice before meditating on their own.
modalities.tweet: Meditation turned into a ladder? No Levels, No Records drops the stages, the streaks and the log: 10 to 20 minutes aiming at nothing, and any lovely state that shows up is not chased next time. A new idea nobody has tested. Keep sits short.

modalities.name: Still Body, Roaming Mind
modalities.tagline: Settle the body once, then let it drop out of view.
modalities.whatItIs: Still Body, Roaming Mind is a new, untested idea that moves Do Nothing meditation as far as it can go from dancing: no movement, no music, no company and no attention to the body. You settle yourself once, lying fully supported, and then leave your thoughts and daydreams free to go wherever they go.
modalities.coreIdea: Dance lets feeling out through movement, rhythm and other people. In this sit the body goes so quiet that it drops out of attention while the mind roams unsupervised, and thinking is not treated as a failure.
modalities.whatYouDo: Take a few minutes to get fully comfortable lying on a bed or sofa, with pillows under your head and knees and a blanket, so there is nothing left to adjust. Then, for 20 minutes, alone and in silence, you let thoughts, plans and daydreams run as they like, without scanning or following the body. If you notice an effort to stop thinking or clear the mind, you drop it.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find body-focused relaxation uncomfortable or dull, and people who believe meditation means emptying the mind and would like permission not to.
modalities.cautions: A roaming mind can drift into worry or painful memories, so if it keeps circling one distressing thing, get up and do something else, and anyone with severe depression, trauma or a tendency to dissociate should talk to a clinician first. You may fall asleep, so do not try it when you need to stay alert.
modalities.tweet: What if meditation let you think as much as you like? Get fully comfortable lying down, stop minding your body, and give thoughts and daydreams 20 free minutes. Still Body, Roaming Mind is only a proposal so far. If it turns into worry, get up.

modalities.name: Every Direction, Sensed
modalities.tagline: Front, back, sides, above and below: only what actually reaches you.
modalities.whatItIs: Every Direction, Sensed is a new, untested idea that pushes insight meditation away from loving-kindness. Metta often ends by sending goodwill out in every direction, toward beings you picture there; this sit turns the same six directions around, and you notice only what actually arrives from each one, such as a sound, a draft, light through the eyelids or the press of the floor.
modalities.coreIdea: Metta pours imagined warmth outward. In this sit nothing is sent and nothing is pictured: each direction is met only through the sensations coming in from it, changing moment by moment, so the space around you is felt as it is rather than filled with wishes.
modalities.whatYouDo: You learn the method from a meditation teacher, then sit alone for 30 minutes with eyes closed and give about five minutes to each direction in a fixed order: in front, behind, to the left, to the right, above and below. In each one you notice whatever comes from there, such as traffic noise behind, a draft from a window or the hard seat below, how it shifts and fades, and you leave it as it is without naming its source.
modalities.whoItsFor: Meditators who find kindness practices forced or sugary and want something plainer, and people curious how much reaches them from all around without their noticing.
modalities.cautions: Close attention to sensation can make some people anxious or bring up uncomfortable feelings, so open your eyes, move or stop if it becomes distressing. Longer or retreat-style practice can bring up difficult experiences, so learn from a teacher experienced with meditation-related difficulties, and people with psychosis, bipolar disorder, severe trauma or dissociation should check with a clinician first.
modalities.tweet: Close your eyes and ask what reaches you from behind. Then from above, below, left, right and ahead. Sounds, drafts and pressure, one direction at a time, with nothing sent out. Every Direction, Sensed is an untested concept; stop if it distresses you.

modalities.name: Rope Between Two
modalities.tagline: Short, all-out rope pulls against a real partner's real force.
modalities.whatItIs: Rope Between Two is a new, untested idea for interval training in pairs, in which two people of similar size pull against each other on a short, thick rope in hard 15-second bouts. It pushes interval training further from loving-kindness: instead of wishing someone well in your mind, you meet a real person's force with your own, as hard as you both can, and then let go.
modalities.coreIdea: Where metta sends imagined warmth toward pictured people, this offers direct, physical contact with another person's effort through a rope, with nothing imagined and no feeling required. Honest effort against honest resistance, then a full release, is the organizing idea.
modalities.whatYouDo: After a 10-minute warm-up, pairs matched by size stand on a grass or matted floor and follow a fixed plan: eight bouts of 15 seconds pulling hard on a short rope from a low, braced stance, each followed by 90 seconds of easy walking. Nobody wins or loses, there is no line to drag anyone over, and either partner can end a bout early by calling 'release', when both ease off slowly rather than letting go suddenly. You finish with a 10-minute cool-down.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find gentle, inward practices hard to feel and who would rather meet another person in honest physical effort.
modalities.cautions: Hard bouts strain the heart, so get a doctor's advice first if you have heart problems, high blood pressure or back trouble, always warm up, and stop at once with chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness. Pulling hard can strain the back, shoulders and hands and a sudden let-go can cause falls, so use gloves and a soft surface, match partners by size, never wrap the rope around a hand and always ease off together.
modalities.tweet: Two people, one short rope, eight hard 15-second pulls, no winner, easing off together. Rope Between Two proposes meeting a real person's effort, not an imagined one. An untested idea: use gloves and soft ground, warm up, and stop at any chest pain.

modalities.name: Relay and Roar
modalities.tagline: Flat-out relay legs while everyone else cheers out loud.
modalities.whatItIs: Relay and Roar is a new, untested idea for an evening of short, flat-out relay races in mixed teams, where everyone who is not running cheers out loud for whoever is, on every team. It pushes team sport away from loving-kindness: support is not wished silently in the mind but shown at full volume, in a real crowd.
modalities.coreIdea: Metta aims to grow goodwill quietly, alone and in imagination, while here support is loud, physical and shared, so cheering and being cheered happen in the open. Nothing is planned beyond the next race, and the mood is meant to be wild rather than tender.
modalities.whatYouDo: After a 15-minute group warm-up and a round of names, players form mixed teams of five or six on a grass field and run relay legs of 30 to 60 meters for about 40 minutes, with at least two minutes between each person's turns. The one rule beyond the race is that everyone not running shouts encouragement for each runner by name, including runners on other teams, and teams are reshuffled every few races.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel awkward with gentle, inward kindness practices but light up in a noisy crowd, and anyone who rarely hears their name cheered.
modalities.cautions: Sprinting carries a real risk of hamstring and ankle injuries and strains the heart, so get medical advice first if you have heart or other health conditions, warm up properly, and stop at once with chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness. Being shouted at, even kindly, can feel overwhelming, so anyone may walk a leg or cheer quietly.
modalities.tweet: Picture a field, short relay sprints, and everyone not running shouting your name, even the other teams. Relay and Roar is a proposed practice where support is loud, not silent. Warm up first, walk your leg if you like, and stop for any chest pain.

modalities.name: One Long Hill
modalities.tagline: One long climb, as hard as you can hold to the top.
modalities.whatItIs: One Long Hill is a new, untested idea that pushes endurance training away from loving-kindness, toward a hard, real, outdoor challenge that kind words cannot soften. You run, hike or cycle up one long hill, alone and with no plan beyond reaching the top, at the hardest pace you can keep going all the way up.
modalities.coreIdea: Metta follows a set script of gentle phrases aimed at imagined people. On the hill there is no script and no one in mind, only the actual ground rising and the body meeting it at its limit, each part of the slope taken as it comes.
modalities.whatYouDo: Choose a long, safe hill or climbing road you know, warm up for 10 to 15 minutes on the flat, then climb without stopping for 15 to 25 minutes at the hardest effort you can sustain to the top, switching to a fast, driving power hike on the steepest parts rather than easing off, with your eyes on the ground a few steps ahead. At the top you stop and look around for a few minutes, then come down slowly and carefully, since descents are where many falls happen.
modalities.whoItsFor: Fairly fit runners, hikers or cyclists who want a simple, wholehearted challenge with no numbers attached.
modalities.cautions: Long hard climbs strain the heart and legs, so check with a doctor first if you have heart, lung or joint problems, warm up, and stop at once with chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness. Check the weather and the terrain, tell someone your route, carry water and a phone, and turn back if conditions turn bad.
modalities.tweet: No pace, no playlist, no plan: one long hill, climbed as hard as you can hold all the way up, power-hiking the steep bits. Concept, not a tested method: One Long Hill. Check the weather, and see a doctor first if your heart or lungs need it.

modalities.name: Set It Down Silent
modalities.tagline: Heavy lifts where every rep must end without a sound.
modalities.whatItIs: Set It Down Silent is a new, untested idea for heavy strength training in which every repetition is judged by one plain sound: whether the weight comes back to the floor, safety bars or hooks quietly or with a clank. You lift close to your limit on a written plan, and your ears, not your feelings, tell you how each set went.
modalities.coreIdea: Loving-kindness grows a warmth inside that no one else can hear or see. Here each hard rep ends in something anyone in the room can hear, a clank or silence, so control under a heavy load becomes plain outside evidence rather than a feeling or a hope.
modalities.whatYouDo: A qualified coach first teaches you three main lifts, such as the deadlift, the squat in a rack with the safety bars set and the overhead press, on a lifting platform with rubber plates. Three times a week, after a 10-minute warm-up, you follow a written plan of 4 heavy sets of 3 to 5 repetitions with 3 minutes of rest, under one fixed rule: any clank in a set makes the next set a little lighter, and three silent sets in a row add a little weight next session.
modalities.whoItsFor: Lifters who find it hard to judge their own control, and people who would rather go by one clear outside signal than rate how a set felt.
modalities.cautions: Heavy lifting raises blood pressure sharply, so people with high blood pressure or heart, eye, back or hernia problems should get medical advice first, and everyone should warm up, keep breathing and stop at once with chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness. Never slow down a failing rep or fight to keep it quiet: let the weight down onto the safety bars or the floor, since the silence rule never comes before safety, and build up the loads over several weeks.
modalities.tweet: Lift heavy and let one sound judge every rep: did the weight come down silently, or with a clank? Set It Down Silent is an untested strength idea built on that rule. Learn it from a coach, set the safety bars, and never fight a failing rep to keep it quiet.

modalities.name: Follow One Out of Sight
modalities.tagline: At a pond's edge, follow one small creature until it goes.
modalities.whatItIs: Follow One Out of Sight is a new, untested idea for small-group sessions at a managed pond, led by a trained professional together with a freshwater ecologist. Nothing is caught or handled: from a safe bank you pick one small animal, such as a pond skater, a whirligig beetle or a tadpole, and follow it with your eyes until it disappears, then pick another.
modalities.coreIdea: Loving-kindness wishes well to countless beings at once, mostly as pictures in the mind. This turns toward one real, small animal at a time, followed as it goes about its life with no wish or warm feeling asked of you, and when it is gone, it is simply gone.
modalities.whatYouDo: Four to eight people meet for about 90 minutes, and the ecologist shows them a flat, safe stretch of bank, where to stand or kneel and what kinds of animals to look for. You move slowly along the edge as your animal moves, quietly telling the person beside you what it is doing, and the session ends with a short talk, led by the professional, about what people followed, what it was like each time one vanished and how it felt.
modalities.whoItsFor: People for whom kindness toward all beings feels abstract, and anyone who would enjoy slow, absorbing time outdoors with a small group and no pressure to talk about themselves.
modalities.cautions: Banks can be slippery and water deep, so stay on the stretch of bank the ecologist sets out, never go in or reach into the water, and mention allergies to insect bites or a fear of insects beforehand. The animals' welfare comes first: nothing is netted, touched or fed, the group keeps quiet and back from nests and reed beds, and the ecologist chooses ponds and seasons that avoid disturbing breeding or protected species.
modalities.tweet: Stand at a pond's edge, pick one pond skater or tadpole, and follow it with your eyes until it vanishes. Then pick another. Follow One Out of Sight is an untested small-group idea led by a professional and an ecologist, and nothing is caught or touched.

modalities.name: Shadow on the Ground
modalities.tagline: A slow form practiced in low sun, watching your own shadow move.
modalities.whatItIs: Shadow on the Ground is a new, untested idea for practicing a short qigong form outdoors early or late in the day, with the low sun behind you, so that your shadow stretches out on the ground ahead. Instead of picturing energy or warmth, you watch the real shape your body makes as it moves: the line of the arms, the bend of the knees and the shift of weight.
modalities.coreIdea: Loving-kindness, and much of qigong, works with inner pictures such as a warm glow or flowing energy that no one can see. This version keeps only what is plainly visible, letting the shadow show the form's real shape and timing moment by moment.
modalities.whatYouDo: A teacher first teaches you a short stepping form of six to eight movements and checks your posture in a few one-to-one lessons. Then, two or three times a week within an hour of sunrise or sunset, you stand on flat, open ground with the sun at your back and repeat the form for 20 to 30 minutes at an even pace, eyes resting on the shadow, noticing where it looks smooth, where it jerks and where the two sides differ, and adjusting only what the teacher asked you to watch for.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who enjoy qigong but find its talk of energy and imagery vague, and visual learners who like seeing what their body is actually doing.
modalities.cautions: Never look toward the sun, choose flat, even ground free of trip hazards, dress for the weather, and if your balance is unsteady practice beside a fence or wall. Unusual mental or bodily reactions during qigong, such as strong agitation, confusion or strange perceptions, are a reason to stop and see a doctor, especially for people with a history of psychosis.
modalities.tweet: Early morning, sun at your back: do a slow qigong form and watch your shadow do it with you, every jerk and wobble plainly visible, nothing to imagine. Shadow on the Ground is a concept nobody has tested yet. Keep the sun behind you and the ground flat.

modalities.name: Let the Jolts In
modalities.tagline: Small unannounced sounds during a sit, and the body's jolt watched.
modalities.whatItIs: Let the Jolts In is a new, untested idea that pushes insight meditation away from concentration absorption. Jhana aims at a calm so steady that sounds stop reaching you; here a friend or housemate in another room makes a few small, unannounced sounds during your sit, and you watch exactly what each one does to the body and how it settles.
modalities.coreIdea: Jhana seeks a stillness that nothing can disturb, so this lets small disturbances in on purpose, and the jolt, the catch of breath and the slow return are watched as passing events rather than failures. Being shaken a little and settling again is the practice.
modalities.whatYouDo: You sit for 25 minutes with your eyes closed while a helper you trust, out of sight, makes four to six mild sounds at moments you do not know, such as setting a book down firmly or clapping once, having agreed beforehand that nothing will be loud or close. After each sound you follow the startle through the body, the jump, the quicker pulse, the tight shoulders, until it has faded, then rest until the next one.
modalities.whoItsFor: Meditators who feel their practice only works in perfect quiet, and people curious how quickly the body reacts and recovers.
modalities.cautions: Anyone with PTSD, panic attacks, a strong startle response or heart problems should skip this or try it only with a clinician's advice, and the helper stops at once if asked. Like other insight practice it can bring up difficult experiences, so people with psychosis, bipolar disorder, severe trauma or dissociation should talk to a clinician, and to a teacher experienced with meditation-related difficulties, before longer or retreat practice.
modalities.tweet: Most meditation wants silence. In Let the Jolts In, a friend in the next room makes a few small, unannounced sounds while you sit, and you watch each jolt pass through your body and settle. Skip this untested idea if you have PTSD or panic attacks.

modalities.name: Tide-Line Sprints
modalities.tagline: Short sprints along wet sand, where the waves keep moving the line.
modalities.whatItIs: Tide-Line Sprints is a new, untested idea for interval training on a flat, safe beach, sprinting along the firm wet sand where the waves keep moving the edge you run on. It pushes interval training away from concentration absorption: instead of one still, inner object held for a long time, attention is pulled outward to ground that changes with every wave.
modalities.coreIdea: Jhana steadies the mind on an object that does not move, whereas each hard bout here follows a line that never stays put, so eyes and feet have to keep reading the water and the sand. The sea sets each step, and a fixed plan sets everything else.
modalities.whatYouDo: With a friend who keeps time and watches the sea, you warm up for 10 minutes on the beach, then do eight bouts of 15 to 20 seconds at near-sprint speed along the wet sand just above the water, each followed by 90 seconds of easy walking back. You stay above where the waves break, choose a calm day on a lifeguarded beach at low or falling tide, and finish with a 10-minute cool-down walk.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find indoor intervals dull and drift inward during them, and anyone near a coast who wants hard effort meant to keep the senses wide awake.
modalities.cautions: Sprinting strains the heart and legs, so get a doctor's advice first if you have heart problems or other conditions, warm up, build up slowly and stop at once with chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness. Sand can twist ankles and hide glass or shells, and the sea can be dangerous, so check tides and conditions, stay out of the water, wear shoes if the beach is rough and never go alone.
modalities.tweet: Eight short sprints along wet sand, where every wave moves the line you run on and a friend keeps watch. The proposed Tide-Line Sprints are meant to keep attention out on water and footing. Check the tide, stay out of the sea and warm up first.

modalities.name: Three in Play
modalities.tagline: Three balls in play at once, so nobody can focus on one.
modalities.whatItIs: Three in Play is a new, untested idea for a fast pickup game with three balls in play at the same time, so players have to keep attention wide and moving instead of narrowing it to one thing. It pushes team sport as far as it goes from concentration absorption: eyes open, constant change, lots of people and no coach.
modalities.coreIdea: Jhana narrows attention to a single object, alone and under a teacher's guidance. Three in Play spreads it across a whole moving field shared with many players who run the game themselves; nobody can track everything, and the fun is in letting that be.
modalities.whatYouDo: After a 15-minute warm-up, two teams of six to eight play on a grass field with two goals and three soft balls, in 8-minute games with short rests, for about 45 minutes. Any ball can score, players call their own fouls, and at each break teams swap one player and say what was most chaotic.
modalities.whoItsFor: Players who get tense or fixated in competitive games, and people who want a loud, laughing break from tunnel vision.
modalities.cautions: Fast play with several balls raises the risk of collisions and ankle, knee and head injuries, so use soft balls, ban slide tackles, warm up and stop playing after any knock to the head. People with heart or other health conditions should get medical advice first, and anyone with chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness stops at once.
modalities.tweet: What if a game had three balls in play at once? Nobody can watch everything, so attention has to stay wide and loose. That pickup game is Three in Play: soft balls, self-called fouls, no coach. Warm up first, and stop after any knock to the head.

modalities.name: Racing the Cloud Shade
modalities.tagline: On a windy, broken-cloud day, run hard whenever cloud shade comes.
modalities.whatItIs: Racing the Cloud Shade is a new, untested idea for hard running with one friend on open, even ground on a sunny, windy day with broken cloud. Whenever the shadow of a cloud sweeps toward you across the ground, you both run as hard as you can to stay inside it, and when the sunlight catches you again you ease to a jog until the next one comes.
modalities.coreIdea: Jhana rests attention on one still object held inside, through set stages and under a teacher's guidance. Here each effort is set by something outside that never stops moving, so you watch the ground ahead for the next edge of shade, with no plan, no teacher and no idea how long each effort will last.
modalities.whatYouDo: After a 10-minute easy warm-up together on a large field, common or gentle hillside you both know, you jog easily with an eye on the ground ahead, and when a cloud's shadow reaches you, you both run flat out with it until its far edge passes and you are back in the sun. You jog or walk until the next shadow arrives, stop after about 30 minutes or when neither of you can make a truly hard effort any more, and cool down for 10 minutes.
modalities.whoItsFor: Runners who find planned intervals dull or too inward, and anyone who would enjoy hard training that the weather decides.
modalities.cautions: Near-maximal running strains the heart, muscles and tendons, so get medical advice first if you have heart or other health conditions, warm up fully, build up over several sessions and stop at once with chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness. Run only on open, even ground away from roads, watch the ground rather than the sky, bring water and sun protection, and head home if clouds start building into storms or you hear thunder.
modalities.tweet: Wait for a sunny, windy day with broken cloud. When a cloud's shadow sweeps toward you across a field, run flat out to stay in it, then jog until the next. Racing the Cloud Shade is an untested running idea. Warm up, keep to even ground, avoid storms.

modalities.name: Walk Up and Lift
modalities.tagline: No psyching up: a five-second setup, then the heavy set begins.
modalities.whatItIs: Walk Up and Lift is a new, untested idea that pushes strength training away from concentration absorption. Jhana begins with a long, gradual settling of the mind before anything else can happen; here there is no settling at all: you walk to the bar, take a short learned setup and lift within a few seconds, with your eyes open on the room.
modalities.coreIdea: Jhana gathers attention inward and lets it deepen slowly. Heavy effort here starts almost at once instead, with no psyching up, visualizing or inner pep talk, so there is little time for nerves or doubt to build, and readiness is meant to come from the plan and the setup, not from first getting into the right state.
modalities.whatYouDo: A qualified coach first teaches you each main lift and a three-step setup, such as feet, then grip, then breath and brace, that takes about five seconds. Then, three times a week after a full warm-up, you follow a written plan of 3 to 5 heavy sets of 2 to 5 repetitions per lift with 3 minutes of rest, and when the rest ends you stand up, walk straight to the bar, do the three steps and begin, while a training partner keeps time and spots you.
modalities.whoItsFor: Lifters who stall in long pre-set routines and talk themselves out of heavy attempts, and people who want practice in starting hard things without waiting to feel ready.
modalities.cautions: Heavy lifting raises blood pressure sharply, especially with breath-holding, so people with high blood pressure or heart or eye problems should get medical advice first, and everyone should warm up fully, breathe out on each repetition, use safety bars or a spotter and never cut the setup short. Stop at once with chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness, and lower the weight if your form breaks down.
modalities.tweet: No pacing, no pep talk, no staring at the bar: walk over, take a five-second setup, lift. Walk Up and Lift is a proposed, untested practice against talking yourself out of hard starts. Learn it from a coach, use a spotter, and warm up fully.

modalities.name: Look Where I Point
modalities.tagline: A silent farmyard wander where anyone can point and everyone looks.
modalities.whatItIs: Look Where I Point is a new, untested idea for small-group visits to a farm or sanctuary yard where several kinds of animals roam, such as hens, goats and ducks, led by a trained professional and a keeper. Nobody talks while you wander; instead anyone may point at something an animal is doing, and the whole group turns to look.
modalities.coreIdea: Jhana is a private, wordless attention fixed on one object you choose and hold yourself. In the farmyard attention is shared, moves among many living things and can be steered by anyone in the group, so you find out what it is like to lend your attention to others and to have them follow yours.
modalities.whatYouDo: After the keeper explains the distances to keep and the handwashing rules, four to six people wander the yard slowly for about 45 minutes in silence, pointing out and watching whatever catches them, such as a hen dust-bathing, two goats butting or a duckling falling behind. The professional then leads 30 minutes of talk about what each person pointed at, what it was like to follow other people's fingers, and any echoes in their own lives they choose to share.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find it hard to share attention, who always lead or always follow, and who would enjoy practicing it among animals rather than through talk.
modalities.cautions: Animals can peck, butt or knock people over and can carry germs, so keep the keeper's distances, never corner or chase an animal, wash your hands afterward and mention allergies or fears first. The animals must always be free to move away and have shelter and water, the keeper ends the visit if they seem stressed, and the talk sticks to memories you already have and choose to share, treats no image or feeling as evidence of what happened and is never used to uncover forgotten events.
modalities.tweet: A farmyard, a small group, no talking: when someone points at a hen dust-bathing, everyone turns to look. Led by a professional and a keeper, Look Where I Point is an idea for sharing attention. Untested, and the animals stay free to wander off.

modalities.name: Leaderless Circle Form
modalities.tagline: A slow form done together, eyes open, with nobody in front.
modalities.whatItIs: Leaderless Circle Form is a new, untested idea in which a small group who already know a qigong form practice it standing in a circle, facing inward with eyes open, keeping together by watching each other rather than following a teacher. It moves qigong away from concentration absorption, toward shared, outward attention.
modalities.coreIdea: Jhana withdraws from the senses into one inner object, usually under a teacher's guidance. This form keeps the eyes open and attention spread across a circle of people moving together, with the timing held by the whole group: nobody leads, and everyone adjusts.
modalities.whatYouDo: Five to ten people who have learned the same short form from a teacher stand in a circle in a park or hall and do it together for about 20 minutes, with no music or counting, letting the pace settle by watching each other. Afterward they stand still for a few minutes with eyes open, then each says in a sentence or two when the group felt together and when it did not.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who have learned qigong in classes and want to keep practicing with others without a teacher, and people who find closed-eye practice too inward.
modalities.cautions: The main risks are those of gentle exercise, so adapt movements to your body and keep up any prescribed treatment. Unusual mental or bodily reactions during qigong, such as strong agitation or confusion, are a reason to stop and see a doctor, especially for people with a history of psychosis.
modalities.tweet: A slow qigong form, done in a circle with eyes open and no teacher at the front: the group keeps time by watching each other. Leaderless Circle Form is an untested idea for shared, outward attention. Learn the form from a teacher first.

modalities.name: Wait for the Bell
modalities.tagline: Sit still, and shift only when the five-minute bell rings.
modalities.whatItIs: Wait for the Bell is a new, untested idea that pushes insight meditation away from dance, where an impulse becomes movement almost at once. You sit alone with a quiet bell that sounds every five minutes, and the only time you may shift, scratch or stretch is just after it rings, so every pull to move has to wait for its turn.
modalities.coreIdea: Dance answers an impulse at once, in time with music and other people. Here every answer is put off to a fixed moment, and the practice is finding out, bell by bell, how many of the pulls you felt are still there when you are finally allowed to follow them.
modalities.whatYouDo: After learning the method from a meditation teacher, you sit alone for 30 minutes at the same time each day, in a well-supported position with your eyes closed, with a timer set to sound softly every five minutes. Between bells you leave any pull to move where it is, and at each bell you check whether it is still there, move once, slowly and fully, if it is, and settle again; sharp pain is never kept waiting, and you move for it at once.
modalities.whoItsFor: Restless people who rarely notice an urge before acting on it, and meditators curious about how many urges outlast a short wait.
modalities.cautions: Holding still can bring stiffness, numbness or pain, so never wait out sharp pain, and people with restless legs, tics, chronic pain or joint problems should adapt the practice or skip it. Close inner watching can stir up anxiety or difficult experiences, so people with psychosis, bipolar disorder, severe trauma or dissociation should check with a clinician first, especially before longer or retreat-style practice, and learn from a teacher experienced with meditation-related difficulties.
modalities.tweet: Sit for 30 minutes with a soft bell every five. You may shift, scratch or stretch only when it rings, and only if the urge is still there. Wait for the Bell is an untested meditation idea about how many urges outlast a short wait. Never sit through sharp pain.

modalities.name: Lights Off Intervals
modalities.tagline: Hard bike intervals in a darkened room, judged by feel alone.
modalities.whatItIs: Lights Off Intervals is a new, untested idea for hard interval training alone on a stationary bike in a darkened room. It pushes interval training away from dance, which is lit, watched and shaped by how movement looks: here nobody can see you and you cannot see yourself, so the session is felt rather than seen.
modalities.coreIdea: Dance builds on seeing and being seen, in mirrors, in partners and in an audience. Taking sight out entirely leaves hard effort to be judged only by breath, legs and heartbeat, and with nothing to look at there is nothing to perform.
modalities.whatYouDo: With a dim night light left on near the door, you warm up for 10 minutes with the main light on, then switch it off and follow a fixed plan of eight bouts of 30 seconds near your limit with 90 seconds of easy pedaling, timed by a quiet beep. You switch the main light back on for a 10-minute cool-down, and the bike's screen stays covered throughout.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who keep checking screens and mirrors while they train and want to learn effort by feel, and anyone who dislikes seeing themselves exercise.
modalities.cautions: Hard bouts strain the heart and training alone means nobody is there to help, so get a doctor's advice first if you have heart problems or other conditions, keep a phone within reach, warm up, and stop at once with chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness. Use only a stationary bike in a clear room, keep the night light on and switch the main light on before you get off, since dizziness after hard efforts can cause falls.
modalities.tweet: Hard intervals on a stationary bike with the lights off: no mirror, no screen, only breath and legs to judge the effort by. Lights Off Intervals remains untested. Keep a night light on, warm up, and stop at any chest pain or dizziness.

modalities.name: Wrong-Foot Games
modalities.tagline: Pickup games where a good fake counts as much as a goal.
modalities.whatItIs: Wrong-Foot Games is a new, untested idea for a fast pickup game in which faking out an opponent, with a dummy, a feint or a sudden change of pace, earns points alongside ordinary goals. It pushes team sport away from dance: instead of moving in time with others, you practice breaking their timing on purpose, and being fooled in turn.
modalities.coreIdea: Dance often builds connection by moving in sync with a partner and the music. This game plays instead with surprise and unpredictability between opponents, so reading people and being read becomes quick, good-humored deception, and getting fooled is part of the fun, not a failure.
modalities.whatYouDo: After a 15-minute warm-up, two teams of five to seven play a small-sided ball game on grass for about 45 minutes, with no referee and no music. A fake that makes a defender commit the wrong way earns a point if that defender raises a hand to admit it, and at half-time each player shows their team one fake that worked on them.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who take being caught out or surprised very personally, and players who enjoy cheeky, playful competition.
modalities.cautions: Sudden changes of direction raise the risk of knee and ankle injuries, so warm up well, build up gradually, play on even ground and stop playing after any knock to the head. People with heart or other health conditions should get medical advice first, and anyone with chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness stops at once.
modalities.tweet: In Wrong-Foot Games, sending a defender the wrong way scores a point, as long as they raise a hand to admit it. Being fooled becomes part of the fun in this proposed pickup game. Warm up well first, since quick cuts are hard on knees.

modalities.name: Nothing to Lift You
modalities.tagline: A hard solo run with every outside mood lift left at home.
modalities.whatItIs: Nothing to Lift You is a new, untested idea for a hard, steady solo run in which nothing from outside is allowed to raise your mood: no music, podcast, snacks, company or phone, and a plain route rather than a scenic one. It pushes endurance training away from dance, where music, rhythm and other people carry your spirits, toward seeing what your mood does over a long effort when it is left to itself.
modalities.coreIdea: Dance often lifts feeling from outside, through a beat and a crowd. With every outside lift removed, whatever mood shows up, flat, cheerful, irritable or low, is carried along and watched while the effort stays steady, and the run is not judged by whether it ends in a better mood.
modalities.whatYouDo: Once a week you run alone for 45 to 75 minutes at a steady, fairly hard effort on a safe, familiar and rather dull route, carrying only water and a phone set to emergencies. When your mood drops you do not reach for anything to lift it, though you may slow down or walk if your body needs it; you notice what the low is made of and whether it shifts by itself, and at home you move on without reviewing the run.
modalities.whoItsFor: Runners who reach for music or a phone the moment a run turns dull, and people curious whether their moods can shift without help from outside.
modalities.cautions: Hard runs strain the heart and joints, so check with a doctor first if you have heart or other health problems, warm up, and stop at once with chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness. A low mood that lasts for weeks is worth raising with a doctor, and running alone means a safe, well-lit route, a phone and someone who knows where you are.
modalities.tweet: No music, no snacks, no company, no scenic detour: a hard solo run where nothing outside may lift your mood, so you see what it does on its own. Nothing to Lift You is a running idea, not yet tested. Slow down or walk whenever you need to.

modalities.name: Same Session, All Year
modalities.tagline: One strength session all year, each weight fixed for a season.
modalities.whatItIs: Same Session, All Year is a new, untested idea for strength training alone in which one written session is repeated at every workout for a whole year: the same lifts, in the same order, with the same sets, repetitions and rests. Even the weights stay fixed for a season at a time, so for three months nothing about the session changes at all.
modalities.coreIdea: Dance keeps renewing itself with new steps, songs, partners and moods. This gives up variety completely, even the weekly rise in weight, so the only thing left to change is you, and the same session may come to feel lighter as each season goes on.
modalities.whatYouDo: A qualified coach writes one session of four or five main lifts, for example 3 sets of 5 hard repetitions each with 2 to 3 minutes of rest, and at the start of each season sets one weight per lift that you keep, unchanged, for the next three months. You do that session three times a week, alone, warming up the same way each time and changing nothing, and once a season you see the coach to check your form, talk through how the weights felt and set the next season's weights.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who keep switching programs and never see where they are going, and anyone who finds choosing exercises more tiring than doing them.
modalities.cautions: Repeating the same lifts all year can overload the same joints, so the coach chooses weights you can lift with good form from the first week, and pain that lasts beyond a session or two is a reason to stop that lift and see the coach or a physiotherapist. Heavy lifting raises blood pressure, so people with high blood pressure or heart, back or joint problems should get medical advice first, and everyone should warm up, keep breathing and stop at once with chest pain, dizziness, faintness or unusual breathlessness.
modalities.tweet: Keep switching programs? Same lifts, same order, same sets, three times a week, and even the weights stay put for three months at a time. That untested way to train is Same Session, All Year. Have a coach set it up, and stop any lift that keeps hurting.

modalities.name: Know Each Hen
modalities.tagline: Quiet bench time in a hen run, learning to tell hens apart.
modalities.whatItIs: Know Each Hen is a new, untested idea for calm, one-to-one sessions in which you sit still on a bench inside a hen run with a trained professional and slowly learn to tell six to eight hens apart by their markings, gait and habits. It pushes animal-assisted work away from dance: no movement, music or crowd, only quiet, careful looking and a few words.
modalities.coreIdea: Dance is lively, musical and shared through moving bodies. Know Each Hen offers stillness, quiet and close attention instead, aimed at seeing each animal as an individual rather than as one of a flock; telling them apart is the practice.
modalities.whatYouDo: Once a week for about 45 minutes you sit on a bench in the run while the hens go about their day, and the professional helps you notice details such as comb shape, feather patterns, who dust-bathes and who keeps to the edge. You quietly say what you notice, and over several weeks you see how many hens you can name on sight; the hens are not picked up or hand-fed.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel unseen or lumped in with everyone else, or who want a very calm, low-pressure way to practice patient attention.
modalities.cautions: Hens can carry germs such as salmonella, so wash your hands after each session, and people with allergies, a weakened immune system or a fear of birds should say so first. The hens must always have space, shelter and freedom to move away, and the professional ends a session if they seem stressed.
modalities.tweet: Sit on a bench in a hen run and slowly learn to tell every hen apart: comb, feathers, who bathes in dust, who keeps to the edge. Know Each Hen is quiet, patient attention to individuals, and it's untested. Wash your hands afterward.

modalities.name: One, Two, Four, Eight
modalities.tagline: The same short form, each round twice as slow.
modalities.whatItIs: One, Two, Four, Eight is a new, untested idea that pushes qigong away from dance: no music, no beat, no company and no improvisation. You repeat one short, set form alone, and each round you do it at half the speed of the round before, until the movement is barely visible.
modalities.coreIdea: Dance follows a beat with other people and invites free expression. Here the beat is dropped altogether and time is stretched inside a fixed form practiced alone, so that as the movement slows, attention has more and more room to rest on it.
modalities.whatYouDo: Standing alone in a quiet room, you do a short form of four or five movements learned from a teacher, first in about 1 minute, then in 2, then 4, then 8, for about 15 minutes of movement in all. You finish by standing still for a few minutes, and you add no music, counting or changes to the form.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who rush through everything, including their calming practices, and want a simple, structured way to slow down.
modalities.cautions: The risks are mainly those of gentle exercise, though moving very slowly on bent knees can tire the legs, so keep a chair nearby and adapt the movements to your body. Unusual mental or bodily reactions during qigong, such as strong agitation, confusion or strange perceptions, are a reason to stop and see a doctor, especially for people with a history of psychosis.
modalities.tweet: Do a short qigong form in one minute. Then in two, then four, then eight. One, Two, Four, Eight is a simple new proposal: the same few movements, each round twice as slow, until they barely look like movement at all. Keep a chair nearby for tired legs.
